name: Palantla Chinantec
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Merrifield, William R. 1968. Palantla Chinantec Grammar. Papeles de la Chinantla V; Serie Científica 9. México: Museo Nacional de Antropología (INAH). 127 pp. (Slightly revised Cornell PhD thesis, 1965.) SIL Mexico facsimile PDF, archive entry 1298.
catalog_locator: §1.2 Phonology, book p. 14; §2.5 The Word, book p. 19; §4.2 Stress Patterning, book p. 38
catalog_quote: Phonological words, set off in this study by space, consist minimally of a single stressed syllable, and may have as many as four unstressed syllables preceding or following, or both. ... Stressed syllables receive either ballistic (ˊ) or controlled (ˋ) stress. Pretonic syllables have tone but no stress; post-tonic syllables have neither tone nor stress. ... Since the stressed syllable is the last toned syllable of a phonological word, it is only necessary to mark one of the two stresses to retain an unambiguous notation. ... Analysis of phonological units larger than words has not yet been undertaken. [p. 14] ... A grammatical word may be (1) a tonic base, (2) a tonic base with one or more prefixes, (3) a pretonic base, (4) a post-tonic base, or (5) a proclitic. A tonic base is realized as one or more syllables of a phonological word, one of which is stressed. Most tonic bases are monosyllabic, and no native base longer than two syllables has been observed. A native bisyllabic base receives stress on its last syllable whereas a non-native polysyllabic base retains its foreign stress pattern. ... Prefixes, pretonic bases, and proclitics are realized as pretonic syllables, and post-tonic bases as post-tonic syllables. [p. 19] ... Underlying the tone-stress paradigms, each base has its own inherent stress. ... By reverse stress is meant a replacement of ballistic stress by controlled or vice versa. [p. 38]
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Palantla Chinantec is not in the catalog. the list of works with stress in the title holds one work under three Glottolog records: Merrifield & Edmondson 1999 (IJAL 65(3):303-323, DOI 10.1086/466392), an instrumental study of the ballistic vs controlled stress contrast; it is closed (Unpaywall/OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar all report no OA copy; Chicago and JSTOR refuse scripted access) and only an LLBA abstract fragment was recovered via a Google Books snippet. The best first-hand placement statement was obtained instead from Merrifield 1968 Palantla Chinantec Grammar (SIL Mexico facsimile PDF, downloaded through the the Internet Archive, scanned at 200 dpi, quotes verified against page scan): one stressed syllable per phonological word, ballistic or controlled, the last toned syllable; pretonic syllables toned but unstressed, post-tonic syllables toneless and unstressed; native bisyllabic bases stressed finally; loans keep foreign stress. Rensch 1968 Proto Chinantec Phonology PDF link located but not downloaded (an automated-access block/the Internet Archive outage). Merrifield 1963 syllable types (Anthropological Linguistics) and the 2007 Merrifield & Anderson dictionary were not obtained. all look-ups used automated download/direct download on APIs and known sites.

'Stressed syllab…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Each phonological word carries exactly one stressed syllable, and that syllable is the stem (the 'tonic base'): everything before it (proclitics, prefixes, pretonic bases) is toned but unstressed, everything after it (post-tonic bases) is toneless and unstressed, so the stressed syllable is always the last toned syllable of the word. Native stems are mono- or bisyllabic, and a bisyllabic native stem is stressed on its final syllable; Spanish loans keep Spanish stress. The stress itself is of two types, ballistic or controlled, lexically inherent to each base and partly alternating in verb paradigms. The language is tonal (an alternative label would be tone language with a stress statement).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; the two 'stresses' (ballistic vs controlled) are contrasting types on the single stressed syllable, not degrees of prominence.
new_statements.exceptions: Non-native polysyllabic bases (Spanish loans) retain their foreign stress pattern, e.g. rifey 'Efrén', kwe.to 'cuento', si.kwé.la 'escuela' (p. 19). Native bisyllabic bases are stressed on their last syllable (p. 19). Some bases show 'reverse stress' (ballistic replaced by controlled or vice versa) by person/aspect (§4.2, p. 38) - this changes stress type, not position.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word, which may realize several grammatical words (proclitic + prefix(es) + tonic base + post-tonic base); exactly one stressed syllable per phonological word, with up to four unstressed syllables before and/or after it. The stressed syllable is the tonic base (stem): prefixes, proclitics and pretonic bases precede it (toned, unstressed), post-tonic bases (enclitic-like) follow it (toneless, unstressed) (p. 19). Palantla Chinantec is tonal; stress here is a two-way phonation-type contrast (ballistic vs controlled) on the one stressed syllable. Based on field data from San Juan Palantla, 1956-61. Data are running text and paradigms, not citation forms specifically.
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes the Chinantec of San Juan Palantla (municipio Valle Nacional, Oaxaca), field data 1956-61 = Palantla Chinantec, pala1351 / ISO cpa. The same variety is called Chinanteco de San Pedro Tlatepuzco / Tlatepuzco Chinantec in Merrifield & Anderson 2007 (the Palantla community descends from Tlatepuzco). Valle Nacional Chinantec (cvn, vall1253) is a distinct but related variety not covered by this source.
